source.title: On the Mechanism and Dynamics of Modular Addition: Fourier Features, Lottery Ticket, and Grokking
source.authors: Jian-Liang He; Le-Da Wang; Si-Yu Chen; Zhuo-Ran Yang

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests modular-addition grokking and its proposed mechanism using a two-layer network, Fourier progress measures, and an analysis of training dynamics. It is a conceptual test rather than a direct reproduction of the original method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own modular-addition grokking results, progress measures, and observations of learned Fourier features. The full-dataset mechanistic experiments and the final-parameter diversification ablations do not by themselves test delayed generalization; the ablations are not included as rows. Results cited from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own modular-addition grokking experiment: a two-layer ReLU MLP, p = 23, 0.75 train fraction, weight decay 2.0, AdamW. It reports train and test loss and accuracy, plus Fourier progress measures (phase alignment, IPR sparsity, parameter norm) across a memorization phase and two generalization phases. This is a different architecture and method from the originals, aimed at the same question. Most mechanistic results come from full-data training, which has no delay.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct but incomplete. The authors also conclude that trained networks implement a Fourier majority-voting scheme, with phase symmetry and frequency diversification cancelling noise. They conclude that each neuron's frequency is chosen by a lottery-ticket competition set at initialization. Grokking, in their account, is memorization through a perturbed Fourier solution, followed by two generalization stages in which weight decay prunes non-feature frequencies.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a two-layer fully connected network on modular addition, with ReLU, p = 23, width M = 512, AdamW, and a 0.75 train-test split with weight decay 2.0 for its grokking experiment. It also studies full-data training and uses Fourier-domain progress measures; this is not presented as an explicit replication of the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the grokking experiment uses a training fraction of 0.75 and weight decay 2.0, and that the memorization-stage accuracy depends on whether test examples have symmetric counterparts in training. It does not report a sweep over training fractions or weight-decay values.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the lottery ticket mechanism, each neuron's winning frequency is set by its initial magnitude and phase misalignment (full-data training, no delay).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which Fourier frequencies a network uses is determined by its initialization, while the algorithm type stays fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: A ReLU-trained model keeps 100% accuracy when the activation is swapped at test time for |x|, x^2 or exp, but drops to about 4% with x or x^3 (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The learned modular-addition solution depends only on the even-order components of the activation.

record.problems: The grokking result is reported for one training fraction and one stated weight-decay setting, with no no-weight-decay comparison or dataset-size sweep. Numerical trajectories are mostly shown in figures without uncertainty estimates. The paper describes some test examples as benefiting from symmetry, so whole-test accuracy during memorization is not equivalent to accuracy on truly unseen points.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size: only one training fraction (0.75) is used.
Whether the progress measures predict the jump across runs, or against controls.
Critical dataset size, ungrokking below it, and any comparison without weight decay or across weight-decay values.
Comparison across architectures (e.g. transformers) or wide hyperparameter ranges.

missing.what: Timing of phases: memorization ends around step 2200 with a perturbed Fourier solution already present; the turning point to Phase III is around step 10,000. This sizes the delay and shows features emerging before generalization.
Two-stage memorization: common symmetric training pairs are learned by step 1000 while rare asymmetric pairs drop to 0%, then rare pairs are learned.

record.verdict_notes: The grokking evidence is a single run with values shown mostly in figures, and there are no ablations of weight decay or training fraction. The reader's V1 and V2 limits_scope reasons cited untested parts (no training-set-size sweep, no cross-run predictive test); these were moved to the untested list. The reader's V5 label cited r5, which is not linked to V5; it has been replaced. Most mechanistic results come from full-data training, which has no grokking delay.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests one training fraction (0.75) and does not sweep training-set sizes, so it does not test whether smaller training sets require more optimization. The reported test accuracy approaches 100% gradually rather than establishing a sudden jump.
Progress measures are tracked in the reported grokking run, but the paper does not establish that they predict the jump across multiple runs or compare their predictive value with controls.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

The paper applies weight decay and relates it to Fourier cleanup, but does not test a critical dataset size or ungrokking below that size, and does not compare weight decay against a no-decay condition.
The paper reports a recurring Fourier-feature pattern across training runs, but does not compare architectures or hyperparameters to test whether they yield the same algorithm.
No controlled tests of adaptive-optimizer instabilities, floating-point limits, or softmax numerical artifacts.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Train on a random 0.75 fraction of the modular-addition dataset with weight decay 2.0
rows.value: The model reaches perfect (100%) training accuracy during the memorization phase; by Step 1000, training accuracy peaks.
rows.note: The paper describes perfect memorization before the later generalization stages.
rows.check: Step 1000 is when common (symmetric) training pairs are mastered and rare pairs drop to 0%. Full 100% training accuracy comes at the end of memorization, around step 2200 (Fig. 11, Fig. 12).

source_check.correct: 100% training accuracy at the end of memorization, approximately step 2200. Around step 1000, common symmetric training examples are mastered while rare training-example accuracy falls to zero.
source_check.problem: The displayed value truncates its timing clause; the supported timing is clarified here.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Track test accuracy over training during the grokking run
rows.value: Falls to 0% early in training; later approaches 100%, with the final approach described as gradual.
rows.note: The text reports a delayed recovery after training accuracy peaks, but describes a gradual final approach rather than establishing a jump.
rows.check: The value is incomplete. Test accuracy falls from 5% to 0% early, then rises to about 70% during memorization through input symmetry, and only later approaches 100%. The rise is therefore not from chance, and the final stage is gradual.

source_check.correct: Whole-test accuracy initially falls from 5% to 0%, reaches approximately 70% during memorization through input symmetry, and subsequently approaches 100%.
source_check.locator_found: §3.3, Principle of Memorization; §A.1, Phases I and III
source_check.problem: The displayed trajectory omits the approximately 70% memorization-stage test accuracy.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate accuracy separately on test examples whose symmetric counterparts are in training and on the remaining held-out test examples
rows.value: The paper reports perfect accuracy on these test examples; across the test set, test accuracy is around 70% during this phase.
rows.note: Symmetry in the input pair lets the model perform well on these examples before generalizing to truly unseen pairs.
rows.check: This is a decomposition of test accuracy during memorization: symmetric counterparts are perfect and the whole test set is about 70%. It shows that part of the test set is solved without delay, not the delayed jump itself.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate accuracy on held-out examples whose symmetric counterparts are not in training
rows.note: This subset distinguishes genuine generalization from the accuracy gained through input-pair symmetry.
rows.check: Baseline is 5% at initialization (chance). The value is 0% on truly unseen pairs while training accuracy is 100%, at the end of memorization (Fig. 10).

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Track test accuracy after the onset of the final generalization stage
rows.note: The paper describes the final cleanup as extremely slow.
rows.check: Onset is around step 10,000. The rise from Phase II onward is reported qualitatively (figure only).

source_check.correct: State: partial for V1. Phase III begins around step 10000; test accuracy already approaches 100% by the end of Phase II and then converges gradually during extremely slow final cleanup.
source_check.problem: The terminal gradual approach to 100% does not itself establish V1's accuracy jump.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Track train and test loss through the grokking run
rows.value: Training loss drops quickly to zero while test loss initially remains high and later decreases; the paper says test loss drops sharply during the first generalization stage.
rows.note: The paper gives the qualitative trajectory but not numerical loss values in the text.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Track average layer-wise phase alignment, measured by average |sin(D⋆m)|
rows.value: Figure only; the text says feature frequencies become roughly aligned during memorization.
rows.note: The paper tracks this as a progress measure but does not give plotted numerical values in the text.
rows.check: Figure only. Rough phase alignment is achieved during memorization, before test generalization on unseen pairs.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Track average neuron-wise Fourier inverse participation ratio (IPR)
rows.value: Figure only; the text says sparsity increases during memorization and weight decay prunes non-feature frequencies during generalization.
rows.note: The authors interpret the increased sparsity and pruning as cleanup of a perturbed Fourier solution.
rows.check: Figure only. The V5 link rests on the authors' attribution of pruning to weight decay; there is no run without weight decay.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Track parameter ℓ2 norm during training
rows.value: The norm continues to grow in Phase II, then decreases in Phase III as weight decay becomes dominant.
rows.note: The authors use continued norm growth as evidence that loss minimization is still active, and later norm reduction as evidence that weight decay dominates.

source_check.locator_found: §3.3, first generalization stage; §A.1, Phases II–III and Figure 5d

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network, M = 512
rows.operation_detail: Inspect learned parameters in the Fourier domain across training runs
rows.value: The paper states that a single-frequency pattern consistently emerges across training runs; neurons collectively cover all 11 frequencies, with doubled phase alignment.
rows.note: This supports recurrence of the reported Fourier solution in the stated setup, not invariance across architectures or hyperparameters. Individual neurons select frequencies through the lottery-ticket process.
rows.check: This observation comes from full-data training (no train-test split, no grokking delay), not from the grokking run. The single-frequency pattern also appears with quadratic activation and SGD (Fig. 14), which is some variation of the setup.

source_check.correct: These recurring endpoint patterns are reported under full-data training, without a train-test split.
